gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX F3000's '3,600 W' is a total: its household NEMA 5-20R outlets are rated 2,400 W max, and only the TT-30R RV port is rated 3,600 W, while EcoFlow rates the DELTA 3 Ultra at 3,600 W output with 7,200 W surge and BLUETTI rates the Elite 400 at 2,600 W with 3,900 W only as 'Lifting Power'.
standout_why: I compared against StormWatts (the cited rival, read in full), PreparedStates and Powersized. StormWatts gives no AC continuous or surge figure and no cycle life for any of its 24 kits. Powersized gives AC for only two kits, with no surge and no cycle life. PreparedStates does flag the Elite 200 V2 and Elite 400 3,900 W figures as lifting power, so the rivals already have part of the AC normalisation. None of them separates the F3000's per-outlet 2,400 W from its 3,600 W total, and none states which capacity a cycle count is measured to. I could not read four pages: the two Dealectric pages, SolarGenAdvisor and Lights On Labs all failed with a self-signed certificate error, so I can't say what they hold.
decides: This weakens ChatGPT's home-backup pick of the Anker F3000. A 3,600 W single load needs the TT-30R RV port, and from the household 5-20R outlets the F3000 is a 2,400 W unit, below the DELTA 3 Ultra's 3,600 W rating. Anker's page also says the F3000 + 400 W bundle ships from early December, so it fails the 'ships now' rule. Among kits we link, the Elite 400 + 2× 350 W gives the most battery under $3,000 (3,840 Wh at a $2,325.60 link price), but it is a pre-order and its 2,600 W rating is lower than EcoFlow's 3,600 W. Only the Elite 200 V2 has a cycle count I could source from the maker with its endpoint (6,000+ cycles to 80%). The finding does not settle the pick alone; the pick still turns on which kit ships now.
